title: Charging a card exactly once
teaches: The two generals problem, idempotency keys, a double-entry ledger, the outbox, and reconciliation

blocks.text: In 1975 E. A. Akkoyunlu, K. Ekanadham and R. V. Huber, writing about the design of network protocols, described a puzzle that Jim Gray retold three years later as a story about two generals.[^generals] Two armies camp on hills on either side of a valley, and the enemy holds the valley. Together they can win; one army attacking alone will be destroyed. The only way to agree on a time is to send a messenger through the valley, and a messenger can be caught. General A sends "attack at dawn". He dare not attack unless he knows it arrived, so B sends back a messenger to say it did. Now B dare not attack unless he knows his reply arrived, so A must confirm the confirmation, and so on. No number of messages makes both generals certain, because the last messenger can always be the one who is caught.

A shop's server meets the same two generals every time it takes a payment. It sends a request to a payments company's API to charge a card $40. Thirty seconds pass with no reply and the connection drops. Three different histories fit what the shop can see. The request was lost on the way and nothing happened. The charge is still being processed. Or the card was charged, and the reply was lost on its way back. If the shop gives up, a customer may have paid for an order that does not exist. If it tries again, the customer may pay twice.

Before drawing any boxes, we must write down what needs to stay true whatever fails. Each order the customer places is charged at most once, and every charge that happens is recorded where the business can see it. A statement like that, which must hold at every moment and after every crash, is an **invariant**. In the rest of this lesson, we will examine a set of designs that keep those two guarantees true over a network that loses messages.

Stripe, the payments company, published its answer in 2017 in two blog posts by engineer Brandur Leach, one on designing an API around **idempotency keys**, and another showing how to build them on an ordinary Postgres database. The design does not solve the two generals problem, which has no solution. Instead, it changes the problem so that the shop no longer needs to know which of the three histories happened.

An operation is **idempotent** if doing it twice has the same effect as doing it once. Setting a field to 5 is idempotent; adding 5 to it is not. "Charge this card $40" is an addition, so a retry adds another $40. The retries with backoff in lesson 18 required the retried operation to be safe to repeat; a card charge is not safe to repeat until the server makes it so.[^http]

The client generates a random, unique key for each operation it intends to perform once, such as a single checkout, and sends it with the request in an HTTP header ("Idempotency-Key: k7…"). On a retry, it sends the same key. The server stores every key it has seen along with the result of the work it performed. A request with a new key is processed as usual; a request with a known key receives the stored result without repeating the operation.[^uuid]

blocks.caption: A charge whose reply is lost, then a retry. Choose what goes missing and whether the retry carries a key, then play it.
blocks.task: Lose the reply, give the retry a key, and play it to the end

blocks.text: With the reply lost and no key, the card network sees two separate authorisations and charges $80. With a key, the API recognises the second request as a duplicate of the first and returns the saved reply without contacting the card network. When the initial request is lost instead of the reply, the key changes nothing, because no first charge was ever made.

The key belongs to the logical operation, not to an individual HTTP request. The shop must generate the key once when the customer presses Pay, store it with the order, and send it on every retry, including retries made after the shop's own server restarts. Generating a fresh key for each attempt provides no protection.

The client still cannot tell the three histories apart, but it no longer needs to. It retries with the same key after a backoff delay until it receives a definite answer. We saw this mechanism in lesson 17 to achieve exactly-once execution, combining at-least-once delivery with deduplication where the state change is applied.

Leach's post describes the server side as a database table with one row per key. The row holds the key, the account it belongs to, a fingerprint (a cryptographic hash) of the request body, a **recovery point** recording how far execution has progressed, a timestamp showing when the row was locked, and, once execution finishes, the HTTP response to return.

blocks.caption: The row kept for an idempotency key, and the phases of one request. Each phase is one database transaction that ends by recording how far it got; the call to the card network sits between phases, outside any transaction.

blocks.text: The fingerprint guards against client bugs. A request that arrives with a known key but a different body (such as a different dollar amount or card number) is not a valid retry, and Stripe rejects it with an error rather than guessing the client's intent. The lock prevents two concurrent copies of the same request from executing simultaneously. A retry that arrives while the first attempt is still in flight finds the row locked and receives an error instructing it to back off and retry later. If the server holding the lock crashes, the lock expires after a timeout so another server can take over the request, using the same lease mechanism covered in lesson 11.

The hardest step is the network call to the card network. Because it is a [[request|request]] to an external system over a network, it cannot be rolled back by a local database transaction, and the server might crash after sending the request but before saving the response. Leach's design splits execution into the phases shown in the figure above: a transaction that records the key and a pending charge, the external call to the card network, a transaction that saves the network's response (advancing the recovery point to charge_created), and a final transaction that saves the formatted response to return to the client (finished). All work between external calls executes inside a single database transaction that commits alongside the updated recovery point. When a retry arrives, the server reads the row, skips any completed phases, and resumes execution from the last recorded recovery point. For the external call itself, the payments company uses the same pattern as the shop, passing a unique reference ID to the card network so the network can deduplicate repeated calls. If the server crashes after the card network processes the charge but before the second database transaction commits, the row remains at the first recovery point. A subsequent retry calls the card network again with the same reference ID, and the network returns its original response instead of charging the card twice.

**An estimate** of the table's size: assume the system processes an average of 300 payments per second, with peaks of 1,000 payments per second. Stripe retains keys for 24 hours, so the table holds about 300 × 86,400, or roughly 26 million rows. At about 1 KB per row including the stored response, the table requires 26 GB of storage. Peak traffic determines the database load. At 1,000 payments per second, where each payment reads its key row once and updates it three times, the table handles about 4,000 indexed operations per second, which fits comfortably on a single Postgres server. A B-tree index over 26 million rows is three or four levels deep, and its upper levels remain cached in RAM, so looking up a key requires one or two disk page reads and takes less than 1 ms. A background worker deletes rows older than 24 hours. Any retry arriving after 24 hours is treated as a brand-new request, which is why clients must stop retrying well before that deadline.

The second half of our invariant requires recording every completed charge. A naive design uses an accounts table with a mutable balance column, executing an SQL update that subtracts $40 from one row and adds $40 to another. This approach has two flaws. First, a bug that applies the same payment twice overwrites the balance in place, leaving no audit trail of how the corruption occurred. Second, the table cannot show the history of transactions that produced a given balance, which every finance team eventually needs to audit.

Merchants in Italy solved this problem by the fifteenth century, and Luca Pacioli published their method in 1494.[^pacioli] In **double-entry** bookkeeping, every movement of money is recorded as two or more ledger entries that sum to zero, ensuring that money credited to one account is debited from another. Entries are append-only and never modified in place. Engineers and accountants fix a mistake by appending a new transaction that reverses the original entries, preserving both the mistake and its correction side by side, just as the append-only log in lesson 16 preserves every event. An account's balance is defined as the sum of its ledger entries rather than a mutable number; the system can recompute the exact balance from the entries at any time, while maintaining a cached value for fast reads.[^cents]

blocks.caption: One $40 sale in a payments company's ledger: the charge, a $1.46 fee, the card network paying the money over, and the payout to the merchant. Each transaction's entries sum to zero.

blocks.text: In the figure, the merchant is credited $40 immediately, the payments company takes a fee of $1.46 (2.9% plus 30 cents, a standard processing rate), the card network settles the $40 a day or two later, and the remaining $38.54 is transferred to the merchant's bank account as a payout. Each of the four transactions sums to zero. Once all four complete, the intermediate accounts net to zero, leaving only the $1.46 fee recorded as company revenue and as cash in its bank account.

This ledger structure allows an automated program to verify the accounting invariants continuously. Every transaction's entries must sum to zero, every account's cached balance must equal the sum of its historical entries, and the sum of all balances across the entire ledger must equal zero. A verification query checks these rules every few minutes and pages an on-call engineer if any check fails, alerting the team immediately when a software bug corrupts the books.

parts.title: Telling the rest of the company

blocks.text: Recording a charge in the ledger does not complete the checkout workflow. Downstream services need to email a receipt, evaluate the transaction for fraud, mark the shop's order as paid, and update analytics dashboards. These services learn about the payment by consuming an event from a message log such as Kafka. As we saw in lesson 16, committing to a database and then publishing to a message log over the network is an unsafe **dual write**, because if the process crashes between the two operations, the database and the log fall out of sync.

The **transactional outbox** pattern eliminates this window of inconsistency. Within the same database transaction that inserts the order and ledger entries, the application inserts a row containing the event payload into an outbox table. Because both writes share a transaction, either both commit or neither does. A separate background worker, called the relay, polls the outbox table for unsent rows, publishes each event to the message log, and updates the row to mark it as sent. If the relay crashes after publishing an event to the log but before marking the database row as sent, it will re-read and republish the same event when it restarts, creating a duplicate in the log. To handle duplicates, each event carries a unique ID, and downstream consumers deduplicate incoming events by tracking which IDs they have already processed, using the pattern from lesson 17.

blocks.caption: Orders saved and events published, with crashes between steps. The two designs fail differently: one loses events, the other sometimes sends one twice.
blocks.task: Switch to the outbox with crashes at 10% or more

blocks.text: A related pattern avoids the explicit outbox table altogether. Because the database already writes every committed modification to its internal write-ahead log, a separate process can tail that log and convert each committed row change into a message log event, a technique called change data capture (CDC).[^cdc] We saw Facebook use this approach in lesson 15, where a daemon tailed the MySQL replication log to send cache-invalidation deletes whenever a database row changed. Whether an architecture uses an explicit outbox table or change data capture, the published event is derived directly from the database's commit record, guaranteeing that the message log matches the database state.

External merchants receive these notifications via **webhooks**. The payments company sends an HTTP POST request containing the event payload to a URL registered by the merchant, includes a cryptographic signature header so the merchant can verify the sender's authenticity, and retries failed deliveries with exponential backoff for several days until the merchant's server returns an HTTP 2xx success code. Because webhook delivery is at-least-once and retries can cause events to arrive out of chronological order, the merchant's server must deduplicate incoming webhooks by event ID and, whenever ordering matters, query the payments API for the payment's current state rather than relying on the arrival order of the webhooks.

Keys, the ledger and the outbox keep the payments company's own records straight. They cannot prove that its records agree with the card networks' and banks'. Every day the networks and banks send settlement files listing each transaction they processed. **Reconciliation** matches every line against the ledger by reference and amount. Most match. The rest fall into a few groups: charges in the ledger the network has no record of, charges at the network the ledger lacks (the lost reply from the start of the lesson, seen from the other side), and amounts that differ. Each group has a fix, an automatic refund, a retry or a person looking into it, and the count of unmatched lines is itself a number to watch.

Card payments also split execution into two distinct steps. An **authorisation** places a hold on the funds on the customer's card, while a **capture** actually transfers the money, often days later when the physical goods ship from the warehouse. An authorisation that is never captured expires automatically, typically after seven days on most consumer credit networks. Separating these steps allows a merchant to verify that a card has sufficient funds at checkout without taking the customer's money before the item ships. Under the invariant we defined earlier, a completed charge corresponds to a capture, as an expired authorisation transfers no money. Both the authorisation request and the capture request require their own idempotency keys, because accidentally sending a duplicate authorisation places a second hold on the customer's credit line until the duplicate expires.

The system models each payment as a formal **state machine**: a payment starts as created, moves to authorised, transitions to captured, and may later move to refunded or disputed; alternatively, it may transition from created to failed, or from authorised to expired if the hold lapses before capture. Every state transition executes as a single database transaction that appends the corresponding ledger entries and writes an event to the outbox table. The state machine rejects invalid transitions, such as attempting to refund a payment that was never captured. A valid refund appends a new ledger transaction whose entries reverse the original capture. A **chargeback**, which occurs when a cardholder disputes a charge directly with their issuing bank, arrives weeks later inside the card network's daily settlement files as a forced reversal of funds, and the ledger records it in the same append-only manner alongside a dispute fee. Finally, to minimise security risk, most merchants never handle raw card numbers at all. Instead, the payments company serves the checkout input fields directly inside an isolated browser frame, stores the sensitive card numbers in a heavily audited vault, and returns a random identifier called a **token** to the merchant's server, ensuring that the merchant's databases, application logs, and backups contain no card numbers that an attacker could steal.

A purchase touches several systems that cannot share a transaction: the shop's stock, the payment, the warehouse. Lesson 20's two-phase commit, in which a coordinator asks every participant to prepare and keeps them locked until it says commit, would hold locks in all of them while waiting on a card network across the internet. Instead, a **saga** (Hector Garcia-Molina and Kenneth Salem, 1987) runs the steps one after another, each a local transaction, and gives each one a compensating step that undoes it: release the stock, refund the charge. If the warehouse step fails, the saga runs the compensations backwards. The price is that the halfway states can be seen. A customer may receive a charge notice and then a refund.

blocks.title: The invariants, written down
points: Each operation the client intends to perform once carries a unique idempotency key, reused on every retry.
Every ledger transaction sums to zero, and existing ledger entries are never modified.
Every committed order produces an event, because the application writes both rows in a single database transaction.
Every line in the bank's settlement file either matches an internal ledger entry or triggers an alert for investigation.

blocks.caption: Seven questions on charging a card once
blocks.task: Choose the best answer to each

items.ask: A shop's request to charge a card times out with no reply. Which explanation of what may have happened is complete?
choices: It may have been lost or may still be running; a charge that completes always gets its reply through
It may have been declined or may still be running, since the network reports every completed charge
It may have been lost, may still be running, or may have charged the card and lost the reply
items.why: Over a network that loses messages, silence fits several histories, including one where the work was done. That is the two generals problem, and why a blind retry can charge twice.

items.ask: Which of these requests can a client safely send twice without an idempotency key?
choices: POST /orders/42/refunds for $10
PUT /orders/42/status with the body "paid"
POST /orders/42/notes with the text "called the customer"
items.why: PUT sets the status to a value, which leaves the same state however often it runs. Each POST creates something new, a second refund or a second note, on every repeat.

items.ask: A client sends a charge with idempotency key k7 and gets no reply. The first try finished, charged the card and saved its reply. The client retries with k7. What should the server do?
choices: Return the reply it saved for k7, without calling the card network again
Charge the card again and refund the first charge, so the books stay clean
Reject the retry with an error, since k7 has been used and keys are single-use
items.why: The key marks the retry as the same operation. Replaying the stored result gives the client its answer, and the card is charged once.

items.ask: A request arrives with a known idempotency key but a different amount from the first. What is the safest response?
choices: Charge the new amount, since the latest request is most likely what the customer wants
Replay the first reply, since the key matches and the key is all that identifies a request
Refuse it with an error, because the same key with a different body is a bug in the client
items.why: A real retry sends the same body. A different body under the same key means the client reused a key by mistake, and guessing which request was meant risks charging the wrong amount.

items.ask: Why does a payments ledger add a reversing entry to fix a mistake instead of editing the wrong row?
choices: Editing rows in place is slower than inserting new ones, and a ledger table is very large
The record of what happened, mistakes included, is what audits and the balance checks rely on
An edited row would no longer match the idempotency key stored with the original request
items.why: Append-only entries keep the history: each balance can be rebuilt and explained, and every transaction can be checked to sum to zero. An edit destroys the evidence.

items.ask: A service saves an order to its database and then publishes an "order paid" event to a log. Sometimes the event never appears. Which change fixes it?
choices: Write the event to an outbox table in the same transaction as the order, and have a relay publish it
Publish the event first and save the order after it, so that the event can never be the one that goes missing
Retry the publish three times with backoff before returning from the request
items.why: The order and the outbox row commit together or not at all, so no committed order lacks its event. Publishing first just reverses the failure, and retries do not help after a crash.

items.ask: An outbox relay publishes an event, crashes before marking it sent, and publishes it again after restarting. What should consumers do?
choices: Nothing, because a log guarantees that each event is delivered exactly once
Keep the IDs of events they have handled and ignore a repeat
Ask the relay's database whether the event was marked sent before handling it
items.why: The outbox gives at-least-once delivery. Removing repeats by event ID where the effect is applied gives an effect that happens once.

summary: **Silence is not failure.** A request that gets no reply may have completed its work, and no network protocol can guarantee certainty for both sides, as the two generals problem demonstrates.
**Write the invariant first.** "Each order is charged at most once and every charge is recorded" is the requirement that every component in a payment system is built to maintain.

**An idempotency key makes a retry safe.** The client generates one unique key per logical operation and reuses it on every retry; the server stores each key's result and returns the saved response instead of repeating the operation.

**The server's key table needs a fingerprint and a lock.** A request with a different body under a known key is rejected with an error, and a retry that arrives while the first request is still executing is instructed to back off and wait.
**Split the work at outside calls.** Each phase executes as a single database transaction that commits a recovery point, allowing a retry to resume where the previous attempt stopped.

**A ledger is append-only and sums to zero.** Double-entry bookkeeping records every money movement as balanced entries, calculates account balances as the sum of those entries, and corrects mistakes by appending reversing entries.

**The outbox eliminates dual writes.** The application writes the event to an outbox table in the same database transaction as the order, and a background relay publishes the event at least once while consumers deduplicate repeats by event ID.

**Reconcile against external systems.** Matching the bank's daily settlement files line by line against the internal ledger catches discrepancies across network boundaries that internal checks cannot see.

**Sagas replace distributed transactions across services.** Each step commits locally and defines a compensating transaction to undo its work on failure, trading strict isolation for availability without holding long-lived locks.

generals.title: Why no protocol works
generals.text: Suppose a deterministic protocol exists that guarantees certainty for both generals, and consider the one that requires the fewest messages. Suppose its final message is caught in the valley. The sender never learns whether that final message arrived, so the sender's decision to attack must be the same either way. Because the protocol must still result in both generals acting together even when the final message is lost, the receiver must also make the exact same decision without receiving it. Neither general's action depends on the final message, which means the protocol works without sending it at all. That produces a shorter working protocol, contradicting our assumption that we started with the shortest one. Jim Gray gave the problem its name in his 1978

http.title: Idempotent methods in HTTP
http.text: The HTTP specification defines GET, PUT, and DELETE as idempotent methods, meaning that uploading the exact same document to a path twice with PUT, or deleting the same resource twice with DELETE, leaves the server in the same state. POST, which most APIs use to trigger actions or create resources such as card charges, is not idempotent by default, which is why the client must supply an explicit idempotency key.

uuid.title: Making keys unique
uuid.text: A version 4 UUID contains 122 random bits. A system would have to generate billions of UUIDs per second for decades before facing a meaningful probability of a collision, so clients can generate unique idempotency keys locally without coordinating with a central server, unlike the short URL codes in lesson 3 that required a shared counter or database collision check.

pacioli.title: Pacioli's book
pacioli.text: Luca Pacioli was a Franciscan friar, mathematician, and collaborator of Leonardo da Vinci. His textbook Summa de arithmetica, printed in Venice in 1494, included a treatise describing the double-entry bookkeeping system that Venetian merchants had developed during the Renaissance. Although Pacioli did not invent the method, his book standardized the practice and spread it across Europe.

cents.title: Money in whole cents
cents.text: Ledgers store amounts as whole numbers of the smallest unit (cents, pence, yen), never as floating-point numbers. In binary floating point 0.1 + 0.2 is not exactly 0.3, and small errors in sums of millions of entries would break the rule that every transaction sums to zero.

cdc.title: Change data capture
cdc.text: Relational databases record every committed modification in an internal log to support crash recovery and replication (as covered in lesson 4), such as MySQL's binary log (binlog) or Postgres's write-ahead log (WAL). Change data capture (CDC) tools such as Debezium connect to the database as a replica, stream the committed changes from that log, and publish each row modification as an event to a message broker like Kafka.
